chapter_title: Direct Connect Connection Types and Speeds
chapter_summary:
As we progress in our understanding of AWS Direct Connect, it's crucial to differentiate between the various ways you can establish a connection. AWS offers two primary connection types: **Dedicated Connections** and **Hosted Connections**. Each serves different use cases and comes with distinct implications for control, cost, and provisioning time. Choosing the right type is a critical design decision for your hybrid cloud architecture.

A **Dedicated Connection** is, as the name suggests, a physical Ethernet port dedicated entirely to a single customer. When you order a Dedicated Connection, you are essentially leasing a port on an AWS Direct Connect router at a specific DX location. This port is exclusively yours, and you are responsible for the cross-connect from your equipment to that AWS port. Dedicated Connections are typically provisioned at speeds of 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, or 100 Gbps. They offer the highest level of control and direct access to AWS infrastructure. This option is ideal for large enterprises with significant bandwidth requirements, existing presence in a Direct Connect location, or those who prefer to manage their own physical connectivity. The provisioning process involves ordering the connection through the AWS console, receiving an LOA-CFA, and then working with your colocation provider to establish the cross-connect. This process can take several weeks or even months, depending on the colocation provider's lead times and your internal procurement processes.

In contrast, a **Hosted Connection** is provided by an AWS Direct Connect Partner. Instead of ordering a dedicated port from AWS, you work with an authorized DX Partner who already has an existing Dedicated Connection (typically 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps) with AWS. The partner then provisions a segment of their existing connection for you, creating a virtual circuit on their physical port. Hosted Connections offer more granular speeds, often starting as low as 50 Mbps, and going up to 10 Gbps. This option is excellent for smaller organizations, those without a presence in a Direct Connect location, or those who need a quicker provisioning time. The partner handles the physical cross-connect to AWS, simplifying the process for the end customer. While Hosted Connections are faster to provision and more flexible in terms of bandwidth, you are reliant on the partner for the underlying physical infrastructure and their service level agreements. Common mistakes here include not thoroughly vetting the partner's reliability or assuming the partner's SLA is the same as AWS's. Always review the partner's offerings and ensure they meet your performance and availability requirements.

Regarding **port speeds**, AWS Direct Connect supports a range of options. For Dedicated Connections, the standard offerings are 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, and 100 Gbps. These high-speed connections are designed for demanding workloads like large-scale data migrations, real-time analytics, or disaster recovery scenarios. For Hosted Connections, partners can offer a wider variety of speeds, including 50 Mbps, 100 Mbps, 200 Mbps, 300 Mbps, 400 Mbps, 500 Mbps, 1 Gbps, 2 Gbps, 5 Gbps, and 10 Gbps. This flexibility allows customers to choose a bandwidth that precisely matches their needs without over-provisioning. It's important to note that while you can order a 100 Gbps connection, your on-premises equipment must also be capable of supporting this speed, including appropriate network interface cards (NICs) and router capacity.

A significant security enhancement available for Direct Connect is **MACsec (Media Access Control Security)**. MACsec provides Layer 2 encryption for data in transit over a Dedicated Direct Connect connection. It operates at the data link layer, encrypting traffic between your router and the AWS Direct Connect router, ensuring that data is encrypted *before* it leaves your premises and *before* it enters the AWS network at the DX location. This is different from IPsec VPN, which operates at Layer 3 and provides end-to-end encryption. MACsec is particularly useful for highly sensitive data where even traversing a short physical link unencrypted is a concern, or for meeting specific compliance requirements that mandate Layer 2 encryption. It's currently available for 10 Gbps and 100 Gbps Dedicated Connections in select Direct Connect locations. Implementing MACsec requires compatible hardware on your side that supports 802.1AE MACsec, and it adds a layer of complexity to the configuration, including key exchange and management. It's a powerful security feature, but it's not universally applicable to all DX setups.

narration.text: In this lesson we will unpack how AWS Direct Connect offers two primary ways to reach AWS: Dedicated Connections and Hosted Connections, and why that choice matters for control, cost, and deployment speed. You will learn the typical port speeds available for each option and how to decide whether you need a dedicated physical port or a partner-provisioned virtual circuit. We will also introduce MACsec, a Layer 2 encryption option that protects data across the physical link before it reaches AWS. Practically speaking, choosing Dedicated gives you exclusive control of a 1, 10 or 100 Gbps port and requires ordering, receiving an LOA‑CFA, and arranging a cross‑connect with your colocation provider. Choosing Hosted means working with a Direct Connect Partner who slices capacity from an existing port, often enabling granular bandwidth like 50 to 500 Mbps and faster provisioning. By the end of the module you should be able to recommend a connection type based on bandwidth needs, procurement timelines, and security requirements, and know when MACsec is applicable. Consider a scenario where a team needs 200 Mbps in two weeks; you’ll see why a hosted partner is usually the right fit.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Dedicated ports give maximum control at standard high speeds; hosted connections offer flexibility and faster provisioning at partner-managed bandwidths. MACsec secures the physical link at Layer 2 for supported Dedicated ports.

screens.title: Dedicated Connections — Definition and Workflow
screens.subtitle: What a dedicated physical port means and the provisioning steps you must manage

narration.text: A Dedicated Connection is a physical Ethernet port on an AWS Direct Connect router that you lease exclusively. This gives you direct, uncontended access to AWS infrastructure at a chosen Direct Connect location. Practically, dedicated means you are responsible for the cross‑connect from your equipment in the colocation facility to the AWS port; you order the connection via the AWS console and receive a Letter of Authorization and Connecting Facility Assignment, commonly called an LOA‑CFA. That LOA‑CFA is the document your colocation provider uses to complete the physical cross‑connect. Because this involves coordinating with colo rack space, procurement, and facility scheduling, provisioning can take several weeks or months. A concrete example: a global enterprise orders a 10 Gbps dedicated port to support a continuous data replication pipeline. They confirm their router supports 10 Gbps NICs, request the LOA‑CFA, schedule the cross‑connect with the colo provider, and perform link tests once the fiber is connected. A common misconception is to assume Dedicated is always faster to provision — in reality, it is slower than hosted options because of physical provisioning steps. Key takeaway: choose Dedicated when you need exclusive port control, sustained high throughput, and you can tolerate longer lead times.

keyIdea.title: Dedicated summarized
keyIdea.text: Exclusive physical port, high control, offered at 1/10/100 Gbps, requires LOA‑CFA and colo coordination; best for steady, high-throughput workloads.

screens.title: Hosted Connections — Partner-Provided Virtual Circuits
screens.subtitle: How hosted connections work and when to prefer them

narration.text: Hosted Connections are provisioned by an AWS Direct Connect Partner who already maintains a Dedicated Connection to AWS. Instead of leasing a full physical port directly from AWS, you request a virtual circuit on the partner's port. Partners can offer a broad range of granular speeds, often starting as low as 50 Mbps and scaling through 100, 200, 300, 400, 500 Mbps up to 10 Gbps. Because the partner handles the physical cross‑connect, hosted connections typically provision faster and with less coordination on the customer's side. A concrete example: a startup needs 200 Mbps in two weeks; a Direct Connect Partner can provision that bandwidth on an existing 10 Gbps port, allowing rapid service commencement. Key trade-offs include reduced physical control and reliance on the partner's SLAs. A common mistake is assuming the partner’s SLA equals AWS's; always vet the partner’s performance history, redundancy, and failure recovery processes. Hosted is a strong choice for urgent needs, smaller bandwidths, or when you lack presence in a Direct Connect location. Hosted Connections — Partner-Provided Virtual Circuits means partner-provisioned virtual circuits with granular speeds and faster provisioning; rely on partner for cross‑connect and slas.. In practical terms, how hosted connections work and when to prefer them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Provisioning Timeline — From Order to Cross‑Connect
screens.subtitle: Steps, artifacts, and typical delays for Dedicated connections

narration.text: Provisioning a Dedicated Direct Connect involves both AWS-side ordering and colocation coordination. The simplified flow starts with ordering a Dedicated Connection in the AWS console. AWS issues an LOA‑CFA; the LOA‑CFA specifies the physical port at the Direct Connect location. Next you provide that LOA‑CFA to your colocation provider, who completes the cross‑connect between your cage or rack and the AWS port. After the cross‑connect is in place, you and AWS test link status and validate bandwidth and jumbo frame settings. Important artifacts are the LOA‑CFA and the cross‑connect ticket with the colocation provider. Real-world delays often come from colocation scheduling, procurement approvals, and physical work orders within the facility. For Hosted connections, the partner already completed these physical steps, so provisioning tends to be faster because it is largely administrative on the partner side. A common misconception is that Digital ordering alone completes the work quickly; the physical cross‑connect step is the gating factor and must be tracked explicitly. screens.title: Port Speeds — Dedicated vs Hosted Options
screens.subtitle: Compare available bandwidths and practical hardware constraints

narration.text: Direct Connect port speeds differ between Dedicated and Hosted options. Dedicated Connections offer standard large jumps: 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, and 100 Gbps. These speeds are designed for high throughput scenarios such as large data migrations or real‑time analytics. Hosted Connections from partners provide granular options that start small and scale in many increments — common values include 50 Mbps, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500 Mbps, and higher steps like 1, 2, 5, and 10 Gbps depending on the partner. When selecting a speed, always validate on‑premises hardware: your router must have NICs and backplane capacity that support the chosen speed and jumbo frames if you plan to use them. A typical oversight is ordering a 10 Gbps connection without verifying that the chassis can forward traffic at line rate or that the NICs are present. A concrete example: choosing 100 Gbps is feasible only if the on‑prem router, cabling, and interface modules all support 100 Gbps. Key takeaway: match port speed to both workload needs and physical equipment capability to avoid wasted capacity or dropped throughput. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: MACsec — Layer 2 Encryption for Direct Connect
screens.subtitle: What MACsec protects, where it operates, and hardware requirements

narration.text: MACsec, or Media Access Control Security, provides encryption at Layer 2 for traffic traversing the physical link between your router and the AWS Direct Connect router. Unlike IPsec, which encrypts at Layer 3 and typically secures end-to-end tunnels, MACsec encrypts frames as they leave your premises and until they reach the AWS router at the DX location. This is valuable when compliance or sensitivity demands encryption across even short physical hops. Currently MACsec is available for 10 Gbps and 100 Gbps Dedicated Connections in select Direct Connect locations. Implementing MACsec requires compatible hardware that supports 802.1AE, proper key exchange and management, and additional configuration steps to enable frame encryption on the interfaces. A common misconception is that MACsec replaces end-to-end encryption; it secures the link at Layer 2 but does not eliminate the need for higher-level encryption where appropriate. Example: a financial services firm using a 10 Gbps Dedicated link may enable MACsec to meet regulatory requirements for link-level encryption while also using TLS for application-level protections. The practical takeaway is to verify macSecCapable via the AWS CLI and confirm on‑prem hardware support before selecting MACsec.

keyIdea.title: MACsec essence
keyIdea.text: MACsec encrypts Layer 2 frames on Dedicated 10/100 Gbps links where supported; it requires 802.1AE-capable hardware and complements, not replaces, higher-layer encryption.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › MACsec
What MACsec protects
Encrypts Ethernet frames across the physical link so frames are protected before leaving premises and until they reach AWS at the DX location.
Scope & availability
Available for Dedicated 10 Gbps and 100 Gbps in select locations. Confirm via the macSecCapable flag in AWS responses.
Hardware requirements
On‑prem equipment must support 802.1AE and MACsec key exchange. Factor this into procurement and configuration plans.
Misconception
MACsec does not remove the need for application layer encryption; it secures the physical link but is complementary to IPsec or TLS.
Key Takeaway

Use MACsec for link-level protection when hardware and location support it; verify macSecCapable and device compatibility before design decisions.

Quick checklist
  • Confirm Direct Connect location supports MACsec.
  • Verify on‑prem devices support 802.1AE.
  • Plan key management and exchange procedures.
  • Keep higher-layer encryption where needed.

screens.title: Choosing Between Dedicated and Hosted
screens.subtitle: Decision criteria: control, cost, time, and security

narration.text: When deciding between Dedicated and Hosted Direct Connect, weigh four core criteria: control, cost, provisioning time, and security. Control: Dedicated gives exclusive ownership and direct cross‑connect responsibility, which matters for strict networking policies and tailored hardware configurations. Cost: Hosted often lowers initial cost and reduces the need for colocated infrastructure, but long-term costs depend on partner pricing. Provisioning time: Hosted typically wins here because the partner has an existing physical connection; Dedicated requires an LOA‑CFA and colocation scheduling that can take weeks to months. Security: MACsec is available only on certain Dedicated ports, providing Layer 2 encryption; if you need link-level encryption and MACsec is supported at your location, Dedicated may be required. A concrete decision example: if your organization requires 200 Mbps within two weeks and lacks a colo presence, recommend a Hosted Connection from a trusted partner. Conversely, if you need sustained 100 Gbps throughput with MACsec at a supported site and full control, choose Dedicated and plan for the longer procurement and colo coordination. Avoid the common pitfall of assuming that hosted SLAs equal AWS internal SLAs; always validate the partner's guarantees before making a production recommendation.

keyIdea.title: Decision guidance
keyIdea.text: Use Hosted for speed and flexibility when time or colo presence is constrained; use Dedicated for exclusive control, very high throughput, or when MACsec is required.

screens.title: Inspecting Connections with the AWS CLI
screens.subtitle: How to confirm type, bandwidth, and MACsec capability using describe‑connections

narration.text: One practical skill is inspecting your Direct Connect connections with the AWS CLI to confirm type, bandwidth, and MACsec support. Using aws directconnect describe‑connections returns a JSON array with entries that include fields such as connectionId, bandwidth, type, and macSecCapable. Look for type equal to dedicated or hosted and the bandwidth string like 10Gbps or 500Mbps. The macSecCapable boolean tells you whether MACsec is supported on that connection. A concrete walkthrough: run the describe‑connections command in the region of interest, inspect each connection object, and note any hosted entries that include a partnerName field. A common misconception is trusting a connection label without checking the type field; the CLI is the authoritative source. If you plan to enable MACsec, confirm macSecCapable is true before ordering hardware or designing the link. This simple audit often prevents misconfiguration and helps you produce the CLI artifact required for course milestones. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.subtitle: Apply decision skills to the scenario in the chapter

narration.text: Apply what you've learned to a common assessment scenario: your company needs 200 Mbps within two weeks and has no existing presence in a Direct Connect location. Start by auditing the AWS CLI to see if any existing connections could be resized; if none exist, reach out to two Direct Connect Partners in your target region and request provisioning timelines and pricing for a 200 Mbps hosted circuit. Evaluate partners by their provisioning lead time, redundancy options, and monitoring capabilities. For Dedicated, estimate the total lead time including LOA‑CFA generation and colocation scheduling; this typically exceeds two weeks if you are starting from zero. A concrete recommendation: choose a Hosted Connection from a vetted partner that can provision 200 Mbps quickly. Document your decision with the partner's SLA, expected provisioning date, and any trial traffic tests. A common misconception is to assume a full Dedicated 1 Gbps will be faster; it usually isn't. The learning goal here is to practice trade‑off analysis and produce auditable evidence that supports a rapid, reliable deployment. screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three essential cards from this chapter

narration.text: Let's recap three concise concepts you should carry forward. First, Dedicated Connection: an exclusive physical port offering 1, 10, or 100 Gbps and requiring LOA‑CFA and colocation work — best for sustained high throughput and fine hardware control. Second, Hosted Connection: a partner-provisioned virtual circuit on an existing port offering granular bandwidth from tens of Mbps to 10 Gbps — best for speed of provisioning and precise capacity matching. Third, MACsec: Layer 2 encryption for the physical link that is available on certain Dedicated 10 and 100 Gbps links and requires 802.1AE-capable hardware. These three ideas form the core of Direct Connect decisions: match bandwidth to workload and hardware, choose the right procurement path based on time and control requirements, and verify MACsec capability if you need link-level encryption. Keep these short reminders with your procurement checklist and architecture decisions.

keyIdea.text: Match connection type to control, time, and bandwidth needs; verify hardware and macSecCapable before committing to a design.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Key Concepts
Dedicated Connection
Exclusive 1/10/100 Gbps port, LOA‑CFA and colo cross‑connect required; best for sustained high throughput and control.
Hosted Connection
Partner-managed virtual circuits from 50 Mbps to 10 Gbps; faster provisioning but reliant on partner SLAs.
MACsec
Layer 2 encryption for supported Dedicated 10/100 Gbps links; requires 802.1AE-capable hardware and key management.
Summary

Choose connection type by weighing control, provisioning time, and security needs; confirm hardware and macSecCapable status with the AWS CLI before ordering.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three quick reminders before you finish

narration.text: Finally, remember these practical pointers. First, always verify connection type and macSecCapable using the AWS CLI before design or procurement work. Second, match requested bandwidth to on‑prem hardware capability to avoid buying capacity you cannot use. Third, vet Direct Connect Partners for SLA, redundancy, and provisioning timelines when considering hosted options. These reminders help you avoid common mistakes—ordering inappropriate speeds, assuming provider SLAs match AWS, or planning MACsec without compatible devices. Keep them as a checklist when drafting architecture diagrams and procurement requests.
